```{r setup-knitr, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

{gratia} provides plots, predictions and diagnostics for generalized additive
models (GAMs). This introduction fits a GAM, plots its smooth terms, extracts
the values behind those plots and checks the model's residuals.

First load gratia and make {mgcv}'s model-fitting functions available.

```{r setup}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
```

We simulate 400 observations with four independent covariates sampled
uniformly between zero and one. The response combines nonlinear effects of `x0`, `x1`
and `x2` with independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2. `x3` has no
effect on the response. This gives us known patterns to look for in the fitted
smooths, including a covariate whose contribution should be close to zero.

```{r data-sim}
df <- data_sim("eg1", seed = 42)
df
```

Fit one smooth for each covariate. Restricted maximum likelihood (REML)
estimates the smoothing parameters, which control how strongly the fit
penalises wiggliness in each smooth.

```{r fit-gam}
m <- gam(y ~ s(x0) + s(x1) + s(x2) + s(x3), data = df, method = "REML")
summary(m)
```

## Plot the contribution of each smooth

Use `draw()` to plot the four fitted smooths. The pointwise credible intervals
show uncertainty at each plotted value of the covariate.

```{r draw-gam}
draw(m)
```

Each panel shows one smooth's contribution. Add the four contributions and
the model intercept to obtain the fitted mean for this Gaussian identity-link model.
The smooths are centred so that the intercept represents the overall level.
For models with other links, add the contributions and intercept on the link
scale, then apply the inverse link to obtain the fitted mean.

The smooth for `x3` lets us check how the model handles a covariate with no
true effect. Its fitted curve can depart from zero because of sampling
variation, and its interval shows the uncertainty in that departure.

Use a {ggplot2} theme to change the appearance of the plots. The `&` operator
applies the settings to every panel.

```{r theme-smooths}
library("ggplot2")
draw(m) & theme(
  geom.gratia.smooth = element_geom(colour = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1.5),
  geom.gratia.interval = element_geom(fill = "forestgreen")
)
```

## Extract smooth estimates and build a plot

`smooth_estimates()` returns the values used to draw the curves, so you can
inspect them or choose your own ggplot2 layers. By default it evaluates each
smooth over an evenly spaced covariate grid.
```{r smooth-estimates}
sm <- smooth_estimates(m)
sm
```
To work with one smooth, supply its label through `select`. Use `smooths()`
to find the labels accepted by the fitted model.
```{r smooths}
smooths(m)
```
Select `s(x2)` to extract the contribution of `x2` alone.
```{r smooth-estimates-x2}
sm <- smooth_estimates(m, select = "s(x2)")
sm
```
Add interval limits with `add_confint()`, then draw the estimates as a line
and the interval as a ribbon. The output columns map directly to the ggplot2
aesthetics in this example.
```{r ggplot-smooth}
sm |>
  add_confint() |>
  ggplot(aes(y = .estimate, x = x2)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci),
    alpha = 0.2, fill = "forestgreen"
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(
    y = "Partial effect",
    title = expression("Partial effect of" ~ f(x[2])),
    x = expression(x[2])
  )
```

## Check the fitted model

Use `appraise()` to look for features the model has failed to describe, such
as residual spread changing with the fitted mean or departures in the tails.

```{r appraise}
appraise(m)
```

Read the panels from left to right, starting with the top row.

* a quantile-quantile (QQ) plot of deviance residuals,
* a scatterplot of deviance residuals against the linear predictor,
* a histogram of deviance residuals, and
* a scatterplot of observed vs fitted values.

The data were simulated with Gaussian errors of constant variance, so we
expect roughly constant residual spread and no systematic pattern against the
linear predictor. Departures from the reference in the QQ plot can reveal where
the observed residuals differ from what the fitted model would produce.

Add partial residuals to a smooth plot to compare the fitted curve with the
observations after removing the estimated contributions of the other terms.
For example, a consistent bend in the points around a flatter fitted curve
can suggest that the smooth has missed part of the relationship.
```{r draw-partial-residuals}
draw(m, residuals = TRUE)
```

## More on plotting, prediction and model checking

* [Customise plots](https://gavinsimpson.github.io/gratia/articles/custom-plotting.html)
  with themes, labels, legends and your own layers.
* [Create prediction grids](https://gavinsimpson.github.io/gratia/articles/data-slices.html)
  to evaluate smooths and fitted responses at chosen covariate values.
* [Check a fitted model](https://gavinsimpson.github.io/gratia/articles/model-checking.html)
  using residual diagnostics and posterior predictive checks.

The [function reference](https://gavinsimpson.github.io/gratia/reference/index.html)
provides argument descriptions and examples for individual functions.
